title: Medieval Indian History
summary: From the tripartite struggle to the Third Battle of Panipat: Delhi Sultanate reforms, Vijayanagara and the Deccan sultanates, the Mughals and Sher Shah, Marathas, Sikh Gurus, Bhakti–Sufi saints, and the books and travellers of the period. SSC asks 1–2 questions per shift, nearly always a pairing (ruler–reform, battle–year, book–author, traveller–ruler), so the tables here cover most of them.

subtopics.title: Early Medieval India (c. 750–1206)
subtopics.concept: After Harsha, north India broke into many kingdoms. Three big powers fought for Kannauj: the Palas, the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas. Then came the Arab, Ghaznavid and Ghori attacks in the north-west. In the far south, the Cholas built a strong empire with a famous system of village self-government.

tricks.title: Tripartite: PPR fight for K
tricks.body: **P**ala, **P**ratihara, **R**ashtrakuta fight for **K**annauj. East, west and south all wanted the centre.

example.q: Which of these was NOT part of the tripartite struggle: Pala, Pratihara, Chola, Rashtrakuta?
steps: The three were Pala, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta.
Chola is the odd one out.

tricks.title: Tarain: 1 to Prithviraj, 2 to Ghori
tricks.body: **1191**, the first battle: Prithviraj wins. **1192**, the second battle: Ghori wins. The second number goes to the invader.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the Somnath raid to Muhammad Ghori.
mistakes.right: Somnath was sacked by **Mahmud of Ghazni** in **1025**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Al-Biruni came with Muhammad Ghori.
mistakes.right: Al-Biruni came with **Mahmud of Ghazni** and wrote *Kitab-ul-Hind*.

mistakes.wrong: Crediting the 712 conquest of Sindh to Mahmud.
mistakes.right: **Muhammad bin Qasim** conquered Sindh in **712 CE** and beat Raja Dahir.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up the two Tarain results.
mistakes.right: 1191 was won by Prithviraj. 1192 was won by Ghori.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the Brihadeshwara temple under Rajendra I.
mistakes.right: **Rajaraja I** built it. Rajendra I took the Gangaikonda title.

subtopics.notes:
### The three powers and the fight for Kannauj
From the 8th century, three kingdoms fought for the city of **Kannauj**. This is the **tripartite struggle**.

| Power | Region | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Palas** | Bengal and Bihar | **Gopala** was chosen king by the chiefs (c. 750). **Dharmapala** founded **Vikramashila** and revived **Nalanda**. Buddhist patrons. |
| **Gurjara-Pratiharas** | Malwa and Rajasthan (west) | **Nagabhata I** stopped the Arab advance. **Mihira Bhoja** (Adivaraha coins) is the best-known ruler. |
| **Rashtrakutas** | Deccan | Founder **Dantidurga**. Capital **Manyakheta**. **Krishna I** built the **Kailasa temple at Ellora**. **Amoghavarsha I** wrote *Kavirajamarga* in Kannada. |

> **Tip:** Say "PPR fight for K": **P**ala, **P**ratihara, **R**ashtrakuta fight for **K**annauj.

### Sindh, Ghazni and Ghori
Three attacks came from the north-west. Learn them as a short timeline.

| Who | Year | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **Muhammad bin Qasim** | **712 CE** | Arab conquest of Sindh. He defeated **Raja Dahir**. |
| **Mahmud of Ghazni** | 1000-1027 | **17 raids**. He sacked the **Somnath** temple in **1025**. |
| **Muhammad Ghori** | **1191** | **First Battle of Tarain**. He lost to **Prithviraj Chauhan**. |
| Muhammad Ghori | **1192** | **Second Battle of Tarain**. He won. |
| Muhammad Ghori | **1194** | **Chandawar**. He defeated **Jaichand** of Kannauj (Gahadavala). |

**Al-Biruni** came with Mahmud of Ghazni. He wrote *Kitab-ul-Hind*.

> **Watch:** Somnath was raided by **Mahmud of Ghazni** (1025), not by Muhammad Ghori.

### Rajput houses and their marks
| House | Region | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| **Chauhans** (Chahamanas) | Ajmer and Delhi | **Prithviraj III**, the two Battles of Tarain |
| **Gahadavalas** | Kannauj and Varanasi | **Jaichand** |
| **Paramaras** | Malwa (Dhar) | **Raja Bhoja**, the scholar-king; Bhojpur |
| **Chandelas** | Bundelkhand | **Khajuraho** temples |
| **Solankis** (Chalukyas of Gujarat) | Gujarat | Somnath, Dilwara (Mt Abu), Modhera Sun temple era |
| **Tomaras** | Delhi region | Founded **Dhillika** (Delhi) |
| **Senas** | Bengal | **Lakshmanasena**; his capital fell to Bakhtiyar Khalji |

Two writers of the age: **Kalhana** wrote the *Rajatarangini* (12th century), the first proper history in Sanskrit. **Chand Bardai** was Prithviraj's court poet and wrote *Prithviraj Raso*.

### The Cholas at their height
The Chola line grew strong when **Vijayalaya** captured **Thanjavur** (c. 850).

- **Rajaraja I** won Sri Lanka and the Maldives. He built the **Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple** at Thanjavur.
- **Rajendra I** marched to the Ganga and took the title **Gangaikonda**. He built the capital **Gangaikondacholapuram**.
- Rajendra I also sent a **naval expedition against Srivijaya**, the Shailendra kingdom of Sumatra and the Malay peninsula. The aim was to guard the China trade.

The Chola navy, the **Nataraja** bronzes and temple building mark the peak of the age.

### Village self-rule: Uttaramerur
The **Uttaramerur inscriptions** date from **Parantaka I**'s reign. They show how village committees, called **variyams**, were picked.

1. Candidates were checked for age, property and learning.
2. Names were written on tickets and drawn from a pot. This is the **kudavolai** (pot-ticket) system.
3. A member could be removed for misconduct.

Village assemblies came in three kinds: the **ur** (common villages), the **sabha** (Brahmadeya villages) and the **nagaram** (merchant towns).

> **Rule:** Uttaramerur + Parantaka I = kudavolai lottery and variyam committees.

### Other regional powers
- **Eastern Gangas** (Odisha): **Narasimhadeva I** built the **Konark Sun Temple**.
- **Hoysalas**: capital **Dorasamudra (Halebidu)**. Temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somnathpura.
- **Kakatiyas** (Warangal): ruled for a time by the woman ruler **Rani Rudramadevi**.
- **Western Chalukyas of Kalyani**: **Vikramaditya VI** fought the Cholas for the Tungabhadra doab.
- **Yadavas**: held **Devagiri** until Alauddin Khalji's raids.

patterns.name: Tripartite struggle and the three powers
patterns.howToSpot: The question names Kannauj, Gopala, Dharmapala, Nagabhata I, Dantidurga or Amoghavarsha.
steps: Place the name in its power: Pala, Pratihara or Rashtrakuta.
Recall the region: Bengal-Bihar, Malwa-Rajasthan or Deccan.
In statement questions, check which dynasty each fact belongs to.
patterns.why: Each ruler belongs to exactly one of the three powers, so the region gives the answer.

example.q:
Which Pala ruler founded the Vikramashila monastery?
(a) Gopala (b) Dharmapala (c) Nagabhata I (d) Dantidurga
steps: Gopala founded the Pala line, so he is not the builder.
Nagabhata I was a Pratihara and Dantidurga a Rashtrakuta.
Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and revived Nalanda.

patterns.name: Chola rulers and their achievements
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Thanjavur, Gangaikonda, Srivijaya, Brihadeshwara or Vijayalaya.
steps: Recall the chain: Vijayalaya, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I.
Rajaraja I: Brihadeshwara temple, Sri Lanka and Maldives.
Rajendra I: Gangaikonda title, Gangaikondacholapuram, navy against Srivijaya.
patterns.why: Each Chola ruler has one or two signature deeds, and the options mix them.

example.q: Which Chola ruler sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya kingdom?
steps: Srivijaya was in Sumatra and the Malay peninsula.
The raid guarded the China trade and belongs to Rajendra I.

patterns.name: Chola village administration
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Uttaramerur, kudavolai, variyam, ur, sabha or nagaram.
steps: Link Uttaramerur to Parantaka I.
Kudavolai means names drawn from a pot.
Match the assembly to its people: ur (common), sabha (Brahmadeya), nagaram (merchants).
patterns.why: The three assembly names each point to one kind of settlement.

example.q: Under the Chola kudavolai system, village committee members were chosen by:
steps: Kudavolai means pot-ticket.
Names of eligible candidates were drawn from a pot.

patterns.name: Rajput and regional kingdoms: house, capital, ruler
patterns.howToSpot: A dynasty, a temple or a ruler to match: Khajuraho, Konark, Rudramadevi, Bhoja, Jaichand.
steps: Recall the table: Chauhan, Gahadavala, Paramara, Chandela, Solanki, Sena.
For the south and Deccan: Kakatiya, Hoysala, Eastern Ganga.
Match the temple to its builder-dynasty before you answer.
patterns.why: Dynasty, region and monument come as a fixed set, so one known item gives the rest.

example.q: Rani Rudramadevi, a rare woman ruler of the medieval age, belonged to which dynasty?
steps: Warangal was a capital of one dynasty.
That dynasty is the Kakatiyas.

patterns.name: Invasions from the north-west: who, when, where
patterns.howToSpot: Words like 712, Somnath, 17 raids, Tarain, Chandawar, Raja Dahir or Jaichand.
steps: Sindh 712: Muhammad bin Qasim, Raja Dahir.
Ghazni: 17 raids (1000-1027), Somnath 1025.
Ghori: Tarain 1191 (lost), Tarain 1192 (won), Chandawar 1194 (Jaichand).
Match the year or place to its invader.
patterns.why: The three invaders are easy to swap, but each has its own dates and places.

example.q:
Muhammad Ghori defeated Jaichand of Kannauj in the Battle of:
(a) Tarain 1191 (b) Tarain 1192 (c) Chandawar (d) Somnath
steps: Jaichand was the Gahadavala ruler of Kannauj.
Both Tarain battles were against Prithviraj.
The 1194 battle at Chandawar was against Jaichand.

patterns.name: Writers and works of the age
patterns.howToSpot: "Who wrote Rajatarangini / Kavirajamarga / Kitab-ul-Hind / Prithviraj Raso?"
steps: Kalhana: Rajatarangini (Sanskrit, Kashmir).
Amoghavarsha I: Kavirajamarga (Kannada).
Al-Biruni: Kitab-ul-Hind. Chand Bardai: Prithviraj Raso.
patterns.why: Each work has one author, and the language or region usually helps you spot it.

example.q: The Rajatarangini, the first proper historical work in Sanskrit, was written by:
steps: It is a chronicle of Kashmir from the 12th century.
Its author is Kalhana.

revision: Tripartite struggle: Pala (Bengal), Pratihara (west), Rashtrakuta (Deccan). The prize was Kannauj.
Gopala was chosen Pala king (c. 750). Dharmapala founded Vikramashila.
Sindh 712 (Muhammad bin Qasim). Ghazni raids 1000-1027, Somnath 1025. Tarain 1191 and 1192, Chandawar 1194.
Chola chain: Vijayalaya (Thanjavur, c. 850), then Rajaraja I (Brihadeshwara), then Rajendra I (Gangaikonda, navy against Srivijaya).
Uttaramerur (Parantaka I): kudavolai lottery, variyam committees. Assemblies: ur, sabha, nagaram.
Capitals and temples: Hoysala at Dorasamudra, Kakatiya at Warangal, Ganga at Konark, Chandela at Khajuraho.

subtopics.title: Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)
subtopics.concept: The Delhi Sultanate lasted from 1206 to 1526 under five dynasties: Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. Exams ask which ruler did what, such as Alauddin's market control or Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency. Learn the dynasty order first. Then attach one signature fact to each ruler.

tricks.title: Who did what: first-letter hooks
tricks.body: **I**ltutmish = **I**qta. **B**alban = **B**ow down (sijda, paibos). **A**lauddin = **A**ll prices fixed. **M**uhammad bin Tughlaq = **M**ove capital and **M**oney tokens. **F**iroz = **F**ields and canals.

example.q: Which sultan is linked with token currency and the shift of capital to Daulatabad?
steps: Token money and a new capital are the two experiments of one ruler.
He is Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

tricks.title: Dynasty order: Sabka Khana Tum Sab Lo
tricks.body: **S**lave, **K**halji, **T**ughlaq, **S**ayyid, **L**odi. "Tum **Sab** Lo": Sayyid comes just before Lodi.

mistakes.wrong: Giving token currency and Daulatabad to Firoz Shah.
mistakes.right: Both belong to **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**.

mistakes.wrong: Crediting Balban with market control.
mistakes.right: Market control was **Alauddin Khalji's**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Iltutmish built the whole Qutub Minar.
mistakes.right: Aibak **began** it and Iltutmish **completed** it.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking every Sultanate dynasty was Turkish.
mistakes.right: The **Lodis were Afghans**. The Sayyids claimed descent from the Prophet.

mistakes.wrong: Placing Timur's invasion at the start of Tughlaq rule.
mistakes.right: Timur came in **1398**, near the end, and it led to the Sayyids.

subtopics.notes:
### Five dynasties in order
| Dynasty | Years | Founder |
|---|---|---|
| Mamluk / Slave (Ilbari) | 1206-1290 | **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** |
| Khalji | 1290-1320 | **Jalal-ud-din Khalji** |
| Tughlaq | 1320-1414 | **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq** |
| Sayyid | 1414-1451 | **Khizr Khan** |
| Lodi | 1451-1526 | **Bahlol Lodi** |

The Lodis were the only Afghan dynasty.

> **Tip:** Order: **S**lave, **K**halji, **T**ughlaq, **S**ayyid, **L**odi. Start years: 1206, 1290, 1320, 1414, 1451. The end is 1526.

### The Slave dynasty
| Ruler | Signature facts |
|---|---|
| **Aibak** | Called **Lakh Baksh** (generous giver). Began the **Qutub Minar**. Built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (Delhi) and Adhai Din ka Jhonpra (Ajmer). Capital **Lahore**. Died playing **chaugan (polo)**, 1210. |
| **Iltutmish** | Real consolidator. Shifted the capital to **Delhi**. Began the **iqta** system. Formed the **Turkan-i-Chahalgani** (Group of Forty). Issued the silver **tanka** and copper **jital**. Completed the Qutub Minar. Got recognition from the Abbasid Caliph (1229). |
| **Razia** | Only woman ruler of Delhi (1236-40). Daughter of Iltutmish. |
| **Balban** | "Blood and iron" policy. Court customs **sijda** and **paibos**. Started **Nauroz**. Created **Diwan-i-Arz**. Crushed the Chahalgani. |

### The Khalji dynasty
**Alauddin Khalji** is the star. His measures:

- **Market control**, with price fixing under the **Shahna-i-Mandi**.
- A **standing army** paid in cash.
- **Dagh** (branding of horses) and **chehra** (descriptive roll of soldiers).
- Land revenue of **50%**.
- **Alai Darwaza** (1311) and **Siri** Fort.
- General **Malik Kafur** raided the south.

> **Watch:** Market control was Alauddin's. Balban never fixed prices.

### The Tughlaq dynasty
| Ruler | Signature facts |
|---|---|
| **Ghiyas-ud-din** | Built **Tughlaqabad**. Died when a pavilion collapsed (1325). |
| **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** | Moved the capital to **Daulatabad (Devagiri), 1327**. Issued **token currency** in bronze and copper (1329-30). Set up **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi** (agriculture). Ibn Battuta was his qazi of Delhi. |
| **Firoz Shah** | Dug canals (Yamuna, Sutlej). Set up **Diwan-i-Khairat** (charity) and **Diwan-i-Bandagan** (slaves). Extended **jizya to Brahmins**. Founded Firozabad, Hisar and Jaunpur. Brought **Ashokan pillars** from Topra and Meerut. |

Muhammad bin Tughlaq's tokens were forged, and both his experiments failed. **Timur** invaded in **1398**, under Nasir-ud-din Mahmud Tughlaq. His sack of Delhi broke the dynasty.

### Sayyids, Lodis and the end
- **Khizr Khan** founded the Sayyids after Timur's raid.
- **Sikandar Lodi** founded **Agra (1504)** and introduced the **Gaz-i-Sikandari** (measuring yard). His pen-name was *Gulrukhi*.
- **Ibrahim Lodi**, the last Sultan, was killed at the **First Battle of Panipat, 1526**.

### How the state ran
- **Iqta:** land revenue assigned to a noble (**muqti**). He collected tax and kept troops. It was not ownership.
- **Diwans:** **Wizarat** (finance), **Ariz** (army), **Risalat** (foreign and religious), **Qaza** (justice), **Insha** (letters).
- **Barids and munihiyan:** spies and news-writers. Persian was the court language.

> **Rule:** Iqta means revenue in return for service, not ownership of land.

### Land tax, jizya and the writers
**Kharaj** (land tax) could reach one third to one half of the produce. **Jizya** fell on non-Muslims. Firoz Shah extended it to Brahmins.

Three historians recorded the age:

- **Minhaj-us-Siraj:** *Tabaqat-i-Nasiri*.
- **Ziauddin Barani:** *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi* and *Fatawa-i-Jahandari*.
- **Amir Khusrau:** *Khazain-ul-Futuh* and *Tughlaqnama*.

patterns.name: Dynasty, founder and landmark chain
patterns.howToSpot: "Which dynasty came after...", "founder of...", or a ruler matched to a dynasty.
steps: Write the ladder with start years.
Attach the founder: Aibak, Jalal-ud-din, Ghiyas-ud-din, Khizr Khan, Bahlol Lodi.
Pick the option that fits both the position and the founder.
patterns.why: The dynasty order never changes, so position alone often decides the answer.

example.q:
Which dynasty ruled Delhi immediately before the Lodis?
(a) Tughlaq (b) Khalji (c) Sayyid (d) Slave
steps: The order is Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.
The Sayyids (1414-1451) came just before the Lodis.

patterns.name: Administration and economy: iqta, diwans, market control
patterns.howToSpot: Words like iqta, muqti, Diwan-i-Ariz, Shahna-i-Mandi, chehra or dagh.
steps: Iqta means revenue assignment for service, not ownership.
Diwans: Wizarat finance, Ariz army, Risalat foreign and religious, Qaza justice, Insha letters.
Alauddin's army tools: chehra (roll), dagh (horse branding).
patterns.why: Each department and each term has one meaning that the options test.

example.q: Which department of the Delhi Sultanate looked after the army?
steps: Ariz means the military branch.
The department is Diwan-i-Ariz.

patterns.name: Sultans' landmark acts and experiments
patterns.howToSpot: "Token currency", "capital shift", "canals", "jizya on Brahmins", "Qutub Minar completed".
steps: Name the act, then recall its ruler from the table.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Daulatabad (1327), token currency (1329-30).
Firoz Shah: canals, charity and slave departments, jizya on Brahmins.
patterns.why: Each big act belongs to one ruler, and neighbours in the list are the traps.

example.q: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency failed mainly because:
steps: Tokens were made of copper and bronze.
They were easily forged, so the scheme was withdrawn.

patterns.name: Foreign invasions and the Sultanate's end
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Timur, 1398, Siri, Mongol, Panipat or 1526.
steps: Mongols: Alauddin built Siri against them.
Timur 1398: sacked Delhi, broke the Tughlaqs, then the Sayyids came.
1526: First Battle of Panipat ends the Sultanate.
patterns.why: Three events mark the ends of the story: Mongol pressure, Timur and Panipat.

example.q: Which sultan built the fort of Siri as a shelter against the Mongols?
steps: Siri is linked with the Khalji dynasty.
The builder was Alauddin Khalji.

patterns.name: Which ruler did this? (signature fact match)
patterns.howToSpot: A list of rulers on one side and famous facts on the other, or "Lakh Baksh", "blood and iron".
steps: Tick the sure matches first: Aibak-Lakh Baksh, Razia-woman ruler, Balban-blood and iron.
Then place Alauddin (market), MBT (tokens) and Firoz (canals).
Cross out the options that repeat a ruler.
patterns.why: Sure matches shrink the list, so the last pairs fall into place.

example.q: Which Sultan is known as "Lakh Baksh" and began the Qutub Minar?
steps: Lakh Baksh means generous giver.
The first Slave ruler began the Qutub Minar.

patterns.name: Historians and their books
patterns.howToSpot: "Tabaqat-i-Nasiri", "Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi", "Khazain-ul-Futuh" or a match-the-column list.
steps: Minhaj-us-Siraj: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.
Barani: Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, Fatawa-i-Jahandari.
Amir Khusrau: Khazain-ul-Futuh, Tughlaqnama.
patterns.why: Three authors cover the whole set, so learn each with its two books.

example.q: Who wrote the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi?
steps: The book is named after Firoz Shah.
Its author is Ziauddin Barani.

revision: Slave 1206, Khalji 1290, Tughlaq 1320, Sayyid 1414, Lodi 1451, end 1526 (Panipat).
Iltutmish: tanka and jital, Chahalgani, Qutub Minar. Balban: sijda, paibos, blood and iron.
Alauddin: chehra and dagh, market reforms (Shahna-i-Mandi), Malik Kafur's raids, Siri.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Daulatabad shift and token currency. Both failed.
Firoz Shah: canals, Diwan-i-Khairat, Diwan-i-Bandagan, jizya on Brahmins.
Iqta is revenue for service. Diwan-i-Ariz runs the army. Timur came in 1398.

subtopics.title: Vijayanagara & Bahmani Kingdoms
subtopics.concept: Vijayanagara was a great Hindu empire in south India on the Tungabhadra river. The Bahmani kingdom was its Muslim neighbour and rival in the Deccan. Later the Bahmani kingdom split into five sultanates, and they crushed Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565.

tricks.title: Vijayanagara dynasties: Some Silly Tigers Attack
tricks.body: **S**angama, **S**aluva, **T**uluva, **A**ravidu. Krishnadevaraya sits third, in the **T**uluva line.

example.q: Krishnadevaraya belonged to which dynasty of Vijayanagara?
steps: The order is Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.
He is the third.

mistakes.wrong: Placing Hampi on the Krishna river.
mistakes.right: Hampi is on the **Tungabhadra**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Abdur Razzaq visited Krishnadevaraya.
mistakes.right: He visited **Deva Raya II**. Domingo Paes visited Krishnadevaraya.

mistakes.wrong: Putting Charminar in Bijapur.
mistakes.right: **Gol Gumbaz** is in Bijapur. **Charminar** is in Hyderabad (Golconda kingdom).

mistakes.wrong: Saying all five sultanates fought at Talikota.
mistakes.right: **Berar** did not join the Talikota alliance.

subtopics.notes:
### City of victory on the Tungabhadra
**Vijayanagara** means "city of victory". It ran from **1336 to 1646**.

- Founded in **1336** at **Hampi**, on the **Tungabhadra**, by the brothers **Harihara I and Bukka Raya** (Sangama dynasty).
- The guru **Vidyaranya** blessed them.
- Four dynasties ruled in turn: **Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu**.
- Its wealth rested on the fertile **Raichur doab** (land between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra), diamond and spice trade, and cavalry fed by Portuguese horses.

> **Tip:** "Some Silly Tigers Attack" gives **S**angama, **S**aluva, **T**uluva, **A**ravidu.

### Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529)
He belonged to the **Tuluva** dynasty and was the greatest Vijayanagara ruler.

- He defeated the Bahmanis and the Odisha (Gajapati) king.
- He won the **Battle of Raichur** (1520), using Portuguese muskets.
- His titles include **Andhra Bhoja**. Another title is "establisher of Yavana rule".
- He wrote the Telugu classic **Amuktamalyada**.
- His court had the **Ashtadiggajas** (eight poets, "elephants of learning"). The greatest was **Allasani Peddana**, author of *Manucharitam*, honoured as "Andhra Kavita Pitamaha". **Tenali Ramakrishna** was also in this court.

Portuguese visitors **Domingo Paes** and **Duarte Barbosa** described his capital. They wrote about the **Virupaksha** and **Vittala** temples (with the stone chariot), the Hazara Rama temple and bazaars of pearls.

### Foreign visitors to Vijayanagara
| Visitor | From | Ruler |
|---|---|---|
| Niccolo de Conti | Italy | Deva Raya I |
| **Abdur Razzaq** | Persia (Timurid envoy) | **Deva Raya II** |
| **Domingo Paes** | Portugal | **Krishnadevaraya** |
| Fernao Nuniz | Portugal | Achyuta Raya |

> **Watch:** Abdur Razzaq visited **Deva Raya II**, not Krishnadevaraya.

### The Bahmani kingdom and its five heirs
The Bahmani kingdom began in **1347** and lasted to **1527**.

- Founder: **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)**.
- Capital: **Gulbarga**, later **Bidar**.
- The able minister **Mahmud Gawan** built a famous **madrasa at Bidar**. Court factions executed him in **1481**.
- After that, the kingdom split into five sultanates.

| Sultanate | Dynasty | Monument or fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Bijapur** | Adil Shahi | **Gol Gumbaz** (Muhammad Adil Shah), the whispering gallery |
| **Golconda** | Qutb Shahi | **Charminar**, Hyderabad (1591, Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah) |
| **Ahmadnagar** | Nizam Shahi | **Chand Bibi** resisted Akbar |
| **Bidar** | Barid Shahi | none to remember |
| **Berar** | Imad Shahi | Did **not** join the Talikota alliance |

### Rivalry and the fall
Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis fought almost without a break. The fights were over the Raichur doab, the Krishna-Godavari delta and the horse trade.

In **1565** came the **Battle of Talikota** (also called Rakshasa-Tangadi).

1. The combined Deccan sultanates crushed Vijayanagara.
2. **Rama Raya**, the real ruler (Aravidu), was captured and executed.
3. Hampi was sacked and left empty.

The dynasty lingered from Penukonda and Chandragiri. Nayak kingdoms took over the south.

> **Note:** The **Group of Monuments at Hampi** is a UNESCO World Heritage site (1986). The Vitthala temple stone chariot is its best-known sight.

patterns.name: Vijayanagara: founders and the four dynasties
patterns.howToSpot: Words like 1336, Harihara, Bukka, Vidyaranya, Sangama, Tuluva or Aravidu.
steps: Founders: Harihara and Bukka, 1336, Hampi on the Tungabhadra.
Dynasty order: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.
Krishnadevaraya is Tuluva. Rama Raya is Aravidu.
patterns.why: The dynasty order and the two key names cover most questions.

example.q:
Vijayanagara was founded on the banks of which river?
(a) Krishna (b) Godavari (c) Tungabhadra (d) Kaveri
steps: Hampi, the capital, stands on one river.
That river is the Tungabhadra.

patterns.name: Krishnadevaraya: conquests, court and classics
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Ashtadiggajas, Amuktamalyada, Raichur 1520, Andhra Bhoja or Peddana.
steps: Court: Ashtadiggajas, chief poet Allasani Peddana (Manucharitam).
His own Telugu work: Amuktamalyada. Title: Andhra Bhoja.
Battle: Raichur 1520. Visitor: Domingo Paes.
patterns.why: Every fact about this ruler ties to a book, a poet or a battle.

example.q: Who was the greatest of the Ashtadiggajas at Krishnadevaraya's court?
steps: Ashtadiggajas were eight poets.
The greatest was the author of Manucharitam.

patterns.name: Bahmani kingdom: founder, capital, five sultanates
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Hasan Gangu, Gulbarga, Bidar, Mahmud Gawan, Adil Shahi or Qutb Shahi.
steps: Founder: Hasan Gangu, 1347. Capital: Gulbarga, then Bidar.
Recall the five: Bijapur (Adil), Ahmadnagar (Nizam), Golconda (Qutb), Berar (Imad), Bidar (Barid).
Match the dynasty name to the city.
patterns.why: The five dynasty names and cities form one fixed list.

example.q: The Bahmani kingdom broke into five sultanates. Which house ruled Golconda?
steps: Bijapur was Adil Shahi and Ahmadnagar was Nizam Shahi.
Golconda belonged to the Qutb Shahis.

patterns.name: Hampi and the decisive battles
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Talikota, Rakshasa-Tangadi, Rama Raya, Raichur doab, UNESCO or stone chariot.
steps: The Raichur doab was the long war zone.
Talikota 1565: sultanates beat Vijayanagara. Rama Raya was executed.
Hampi is a UNESCO site. The stone chariot is at the Vitthala temple.
patterns.why: One battle (Talikota) and one man (Rama Raya) end the empire.

example.q: Who led Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota (1565) and was executed after defeat?
steps: Talikota was fought in 1565.
The Aravidu regent Rama Raya was captured and executed.

patterns.name: Monuments of the Deccan sultanates
patterns.howToSpot: "Gol Gumbaz is in", "Charminar was built by", "Chand Bibi".
steps: Bijapur: Gol Gumbaz (Muhammad Adil Shah), whispering gallery.
Golconda: Charminar, Hyderabad, 1591 (Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah).
Ahmadnagar: Chand Bibi resisted Akbar.
patterns.why: Each sultanate has one famous monument or person.

example.q: The Gol Gumbaz, with its whispering gallery, is in which city?
steps: Gol Gumbaz was built by Muhammad Adil Shah.
The Adil Shahis ruled Bijapur.

patterns.name: Foreign visitors to Vijayanagara
patterns.howToSpot: "Who visited the court of..." with names such as Razzaq, Paes, Conti or Nuniz.
steps: Conti (Italy): Deva Raya I.
Abdur Razzaq (Persia): Deva Raya II.
Paes (Portugal): Krishnadevaraya. Nuniz (Portugal): Achyuta Raya.
patterns.why: Each traveller pairs with one ruler, so the country also helps.

example.q: Which foreign visitor came as a Persian envoy to Deva Raya II?
steps: Persia narrows the list.
The Timurid envoy was Abdur Razzaq.

revision: 1336: Harihara and Bukka (Sangama) at Hampi. Guru: Vidyaranya.
Dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.
Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva): Raichur 1520, Ashtadiggajas, Allasani Peddana, Amuktamalyada.
Bahmani: Hasan Gangu, 1347, Gulbarga then Bidar. Mahmud Gawan was executed in 1481.
Five sultanates: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Berar, Bidar.
1565 Talikota: Rama Raya killed, Hampi sacked. Hampi is now a UNESCO site.

subtopics.title: Mughal Empire & Sher Shah Suri
subtopics.concept: The Mughal empire began with Babur's win at Panipat in 1526. Sher Shah Suri broke it for a few years, then Akbar built it up. Shah Jahan gave it great buildings, and Aurangzeb's long wars weakened it. Exams ask which emperor did what, plus the key battles and revenue terms.

tricks.title: Mughal order: Bahut Hi Accha Jalebi Shahi Aur
tricks.body: **B**abur, **H**umayun, **A**kbar, **J**ahangir, **S**hah Jahan, **A**urangzeb. Sher Shah sits between Humayun's two reigns (1540-55).

example.q: Which ruler came between Humayun's two reigns?
steps: Humayun lost in 1540 and returned in 1555.
Sher Shah ruled in between.

tricks.title: Three Panipats: 26, 56, 61
tricks.body: **1526** Babur beats Ibrahim Lodi. **1556** Akbar's side (Bairam Khan) beats Hemu. **1761** Ahmad Shah Abdali beats the Marathas.

mistakes.wrong: Crediting Akbar with the rupiya.
mistakes.right: **Sher Shah** issued the silver rupiya and copper dam.

mistakes.wrong: Swapping Din-i-Ilahi and Ibadat Khana dates.
mistakes.right: Ibadat Khana = **1575**. Din-i-Ilahi = **1582**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Akbar himself led at Haldighati.
mistakes.right: The Mughal commander was **Man Singh**.

mistakes.wrong: Giving Itimad-ud-Daulah to Shah Jahan.
mistakes.right: **Nur Jahan** built it. The Taj Mahal is Shah Jahan's.

mistakes.wrong: Placing Chausa and Kannauj under Babur.
mistakes.right: Both are **Humayun's** defeats by Sher Shah (1539, 1540).

subtopics.notes:
### Babur and Humayun (1526-1556)
| Ruler | Years | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Babur** | 1526-30 | **First Battle of Panipat** (21 April 1526) against **Ibrahim Lodi**. First use of field guns in India. Also **Khanwa** (1527, against **Rana Sanga**), **Chanderi** (1528, Medini Rai) and **Ghaghra** (1529). Wrote the *Baburnama* (*Tuzuk-i-Baburi*) in **Turki**. |
| **Humayun** | 1530-40, 1555-56 | Lost to Sher Shah at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kannauj / Bilgram (1540)**. Won Delhi back in 1555. Died falling from the stairs of his library, **Sher Mandal**. |

Babur was a Chagatai Timurid from Fergana. At Panipat he used artillery and the *tulughma* (encircling) tactic. Humayun wandered for 15 years and returned with help from Persia.

### Sher Shah Suri (1540-1545)
He was an Afghan from Sasaram. He ruled well in only five years.

- Issued the silver **rupiya** and the copper **dam**.
- Rebuilt the **Grand Trunk Road** from Sonargaon in Bengal to Peshawar, with **sarais** (rest houses) at stages.
- Set up land measurement, **patta** (title deed) and **qabuliyat** (agreement deed).
- Ran a spy-based administration.
- His tomb is at **Sasaram (Bihar)**. He died at **Kalinjar**.

> **Watch:** The rupiya came from **Sher Shah**, not Akbar.

### Akbar (1556-1605)
**Bairam Khan**, the regent, won the **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** against **Hemu**. Then Akbar acted on many fronts.

- **Conquests:** Malwa, Chittor (1568), Ranthambhor, Gujarat and Bengal. **Buland Darwaza** marks the Gujarat win.
- **Haldighati (1576):** Mughal army under **Man Singh** against **Maharana Pratap**.
- **Rajput policy:** alliances and marriages with Amber. Man Singh and Todar Mal served at high rank.
- **Tolerance:** abolished the pilgrim tax and **jizya (1564)**.
- **Religion:** **Ibadat Khana** at Fatehpur Sikri (1575). **Din-i-Ilahi** (1582), a mixed order.
- **Court:** the **Navaratna** circle included Birbal, Todar Mal, Abul Fazl, Faizi, Tansen and Man Singh.

> **Tip:** Ibadat Khana comes first (**1575**). Din-i-Ilahi follows (**1582**).

### Akbar's system
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Mansab** | Rank fixed by **zat** (personal rank) and **sawar** (cavalry count) |
| **Jagir** | Revenue assignment given to a mansabdar instead of salary |
| **Zabti / Dahsala** | Revenue system of **Raja Todar Mal**, based on a 10-year average |
| **Subah / Sarkar / Pargana** | Province / district / sub-district |
| **Diwan / Mir Bakshi** | Finance / military pay and intelligence |

### Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb
| Ruler | Years | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Jahangir** | 1605-27 | **Chain of justice** (Zanjir-i-Adl). **Nur Jahan** ran the court. English envoys **Hawkins (1608)** and **Sir Thomas Roe (1615)**. Executed **Guru Arjan Dev (1606)**. *Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri*. |
| **Shah Jahan** | 1628-58 | **Taj Mahal** for Mumtaz Mahal. **Red Fort** and **Jama Masjid**, Delhi (Shahjahanabad). **Peacock Throne**. |
| **Aurangzeb** | 1658-1707 | Re-imposed **jizya (1679)**. Executed **Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675)**. Fought the Marathas in the Deccan for 25 years. Died at Ahmednagar, buried at **Khuldabad**. |

### Buildings in pairs
- **Humayun's Tomb** (Delhi): first garden-tomb on the subcontinent.
- **Itimad-ud-Daulah** (Agra): built by **Nur Jahan** for her father. Early pietra dura in white marble.
- **Fatehpur Sikri:** Akbar's city, with the Panch Mahal and Jodha Bai palace.

### Later Mughals
Later kings were puppets. The **Sayyid brothers** made and unmade them. **Nadir Shah** of Persia invaded in **1739** (Battle of **Karnal**) under **Muhammad Shah "Rangila"**. He took the **Peacock Throne** and the **Koh-i-Noor**. **Ahmad Shah Abdali** raided again and again.

patterns.name: Babur, Humayun and Sher Shah: battles and reforms
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Panipat 1526, Khanwa, Chausa, Kannauj, rupiya, Grand Trunk Road or Sasaram.
steps: Babur: Panipat 1526 (Lodi), Khanwa 1527 (Rana Sanga).
Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa 1539 and Kannauj 1540.
Sher Shah: rupiya, dam, GT Road with sarais, patta-qabuliyat.
patterns.why: The battles form a chain, and Sher Shah's reforms sit between Humayun's two reigns.

example.q: The Grand Trunk Road revived by Sher Shah connected the north-west with:
steps: It ran to Peshawar in the north-west.
The other end was Sonargaon in Bengal.

patterns.name: Akbar: conquests, administration and Din-i-Ilahi
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Hemu, dahsala, zat, sawar, Ibadat Khana, Din-i-Ilahi, jizya or Todar Mal.
steps: Second Panipat 1556: Bairam Khan beat Hemu.
Revenue: Todar Mal's dahsala. Ranks: zat and sawar.
Ideas: Din-i-Ilahi 1582, Ibadat Khana 1575, jizya abolished 1564.
patterns.why: Each Akbar reform has one name and one year, and options swap them.

example.q: Who devised the dahsala (zabti) revenue system of Akbar's reign?
steps: Dahsala means ten-year average.
Akbar's finance minister set it.

patterns.name: Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb
patterns.howToSpot: Words like chain of justice, Roe, Peacock Throne, Taj Mahal, jizya 1679 or Tegh Bahadur.
steps: Jahangir: chain of justice, Roe 1615, Nur Jahan, Guru Arjan 1606.
Shah Jahan: Peacock Throne, Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid.
Aurangzeb: jizya 1679, Guru Tegh Bahadur 1675, Deccan wars.
patterns.why: Each of the three emperors has a clear set of signature facts.

example.q: Who came as ambassador of England's James I to Jahangir's court in 1615?
steps: Hawkins came earlier, in 1608.
The 1615 envoy was Sir Thomas Roe.

patterns.name: Later Mughals and the empire's decline
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Nadir Shah, Karnal, Rangila, Sayyid brothers, Koh-i-Noor or Abdali.
steps: Nadir Shah, 1739: won at Karnal, took Koh-i-Noor and Peacock Throne.
The ruler then was Muhammad Shah Rangila.
Sayyid brothers were king-makers. Abdali raided repeatedly.
patterns.why: One invasion (1739) and one ruler (Muhammad Shah) answer most questions.

example.q: Nadir Shah invaded India in 1739 during the reign of:
steps: Battle of Karnal was in 1739.
The Mughal king was Muhammad Shah Rangila.

patterns.name: Mughal administration terms
patterns.howToSpot: Words like mansab, zat, sawar, jagir, subah, sarkar, pargana or Mir Bakshi.
steps: Mansab = rank. Zat = personal rank. Sawar = cavalry count.
Jagir = revenue assignment instead of salary.
Order of areas: subah (province), sarkar (district), pargana (sub-district).
patterns.why: The terms come in small sets, and the options mix their meanings.

example.q: In the Mughal mansabdari system, "sawar" stood for:
steps: Zat was personal rank.
Sawar was the number of cavalry.

patterns.name: Buildings and their builders
patterns.howToSpot: "Taj Mahal", "Itimad-ud-Daulah", "Buland Darwaza", "Humayun's Tomb", "Sher Mandal".
steps: Shah Jahan: Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid.
Nur Jahan: Itimad-ud-Daulah. Akbar: Fatehpur Sikri, Buland Darwaza.
Sasaram tomb: Sher Shah. Humayun's Tomb: first garden-tomb.
patterns.why: Each monument has one patron, and the options swap them.

example.q: Itimad-ud-Daulah at Agra was built by Nur Jahan for:
steps: It honours her father.
It shows early pietra dura in white marble.

revision: Babur: Panipat 1526, Khanwa 1527. Baburnama in Turki. Humayun: Chausa 1539, Kannauj 1540.
Sher Shah: rupiya, dam, Grand Trunk Road with sarais, patta and qabuliyat, tomb at Sasaram.
Akbar: Second Panipat 1556, jizya abolished 1564, Ibadat Khana 1575, Din-i-Ilahi 1582.
Todar Mal: dahsala (zabti). Mansab has zat and sawar.
Jahangir: chain of justice, Roe 1615. Shah Jahan: Peacock Throne, Taj. Aurangzeb: jizya 1679, Tegh Bahadur 1675.
1739: Nadir Shah at Karnal, under Muhammad Shah Rangila.

subtopics.title: Marathas & Sikh Gurus
subtopics.concept: Shivaji built the Maratha state in the 1600s with hill forts and fast cavalry. After him the Peshwas led a confederacy until the British ended it in 1818. The ten Sikh Gurus shaped the Sikh faith, and Ranjit Singh built a Sikh kingdom at Lahore.

tricks.title: Guru order: Nana Aur Amar Ram Arjun, Har-Har-Har Tegh Gobind
tricks.body: **N**anak, **A**ngad, **Amar** Das, **Ram** Das, **Arjan**, then the three Hars (Har**gobind**, **Har** Rai, **Har** Krishan), then **Tegh** Bahadur, then **Gobind** Singh.

example.q: Who was the ninth Sikh Guru?
steps: The three Hars are 6, 7 and 8.
Tegh Bahadur comes next.

tricks.title: Chauth vs Sardeshmukhi
tricks.body: **Ch**auth = **Ch**aar ana in the rupee (1/4). Sardeshmukhi = 10%, the tenth claimed by the hereditary head.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the Adi Granth to Guru Gobind Singh.
mistakes.right: **Guru Arjan Dev** compiled it. Gobind Singh founded the **Khalsa**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Jahangir executed Guru Tegh Bahadur.
mistakes.right: Jahangir executed **Arjan Dev** (1606). **Aurangzeb** executed Tegh Bahadur (1675).

mistakes.wrong: Naming Nadir Shah as the winner at Third Panipat.
mistakes.right: The winner was **Ahmad Shah Abdali**. Nadir Shah invaded in 1739.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing chauth and sardeshmukhi.
mistakes.right: Chauth is **25%**. Sardeshmukhi is an extra **10%**.

subtopics.notes:
### Shivaji builds a kingdom
**Shivaji** was born in **1630** at **Shivneri**. His father was Shahaji and his mother **Jijabai**. He built a state out of Bijapur's Deccan land with hill forts and light cavalry.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **1659** | Killed Bijapur general **Afzal Khan** at **Pratapgarh** |
| **1665** | **Treaty of Purandar** with **Raja Jai Singh**. He gave up 23 forts. |
| **1666** | Visit to Agra and escape |
| **1674** | Crowned **Chhatrapati** at **Raigad**. Gaga Bhatt led the rituals. |

Forts of note: Torna, Rajgad, Sinhagad. **Tanaji Malusare** fell at Sinhagad. Shivaji also raided Surat and humbled Shaista Khan at Pune.

Revenue used **kathi** assessment. The army was paid in cash. Two taxes are asked often: **chauth** (**1/4**, 25% of revenue) and **sardeshmukhi** (an extra **10%**).

### Shivaji's Ashtapradhan
| Post | Portfolio |
|---|---|
| **Peshwa** | Prime Minister |
| **Amatya** (Majumdar) | Finance and accounts |
| **Mantri** (Waqia-navis) | Daily records, the king's diary |
| **Sachiv** (Shurunavis) | Royal letters |
| **Sumant** (Dabir) | **Foreign affairs** |
| **Senapati** (Sar-i-Naubat) | Army |
| **Panditrao** | Religious matters |
| **Nyayadhish** | Justice |

> **Tip:** Chauth = **Ch**aar ana in a rupee (1/4). Sardeshmukhi is 10%.

### The Peshwas and the confederacy
- **Balaji Vishwanath** was the first Peshwa of the Bhat family (1713).
- **Baji Rao I** (1720-40) was the greatest cavalry general. He took Maratha arms to Malwa, Bundelkhand and Delhi's gates.
- **Balaji Baji Rao** (Nana Saheb) saw the **Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761)**. **Ahmad Shah Abdali** beat the Marathas under **Sadashivrao Bhau**.

After that, power lay with the confederacy houses under the Peshwa at Pune.

| House | Seat |
|---|---|
| **Scindia** | Gwalior |
| **Holkar** | Indore |
| **Gaekwad** | Baroda |
| **Bhonsle** | Nagpur |

Three Anglo-Maratha wars followed. The **Treaty of Salbai (1782)** ended the first. **Baji Rao II** signed the **Treaty of Bassein (1802)**, a subsidiary alliance, and the second war began. The third war (1817-18) ended Maratha power.

### The ten Sikh Gurus
| # | Guru | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Nanak** | Founder. Born 1469 at **Talwandi** (Nankana Sahib). One God, **langar**, honest work. |
| 2 | **Angad** | Standardised the **Gurmukhi** script |
| 3 | **Amar Das** | Manji system; strengthened langar |
| 4 | **Ram Das** | Founded **Amritsar** (Ramdaspur) |
| 5 | **Arjan Dev** | Compiled the **Adi Granth (1604)**. Built Harmandir Sahib. Executed by **Jahangir (1606)**. |
| 6 | **Hargobind** | **Akal Takht**; Miri-Piri, the armed saint |
| 7 | **Har Rai** | none to remember |
| 8 | **Har Krishan** | Youngest guru |
| 9 | **Tegh Bahadur** | Executed by **Aurangzeb (1675)** in Delhi |
| 10 | **Gobind Singh** | Founded the **Khalsa (1699)** at **Anandpur Sahib** on Baisakhi. Declared the Granth the eternal Guru. |

> **Watch:** Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth. Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa. Arjan died under Jahangir, Tegh Bahadur under Aurangzeb.

### After the tenth Guru
**Banda Bahadur** carried on the Khalsa fight and was executed in **1716**. Sikh **misls** (confederacies) followed. **Maharaja Ranjit Singh** of the **Sukerchakia misl** took **Lahore in 1799**. He ruled Punjab until 1839 and was called **Sher-e-Punjab**. The Khalsa's five K's are kesh, kangha, kara, kachchha and kirpan.

patterns.name: Shivaji: conquests, treaty, coronation, Ashtapradhan
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Afzal Khan, Purandar, Raigad, Chhatrapati, Ashtapradhan or Sumant.
steps: Chain: Pratapgarh 1659, Purandar 1665, Agra 1666, Raigad 1674.
Purandar was with Jai Singh (23 forts).
Ashtapradhan: Peshwa, Senapati, Amatya, Sumant (foreign), Nyayadhish.
patterns.why: The four dates make one story, and each has one place.

example.q:
Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674 at:
(a) Pratapgarh (b) Raigad (c) Purandar (d) Shivneri
steps: Shivneri was his birthplace.
Pratapgarh was the Afzal Khan fight and Purandar the treaty.
The coronation was at Raigad.

patterns.name: Peshwas, confederacy houses and Anglo-Maratha wars
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao, Scindia, Holkar, Salbai or Bassein.
steps: Peshwa order: Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I, Balaji Baji Rao.
Houses: Scindia-Gwalior, Holkar-Indore, Gaekwad-Baroda, Bhonsle-Nagpur.
Wars: Salbai 1782 ends the first; Bassein 1802 starts the second; 1818 ends the third.
patterns.why: Names, seats and treaties each come as a fixed set.

example.q: Which Maratha confederacy house was based at Gwalior?
steps: Holkar was at Indore.
Gaekwad was at Baroda.
Gwalior belonged to the Scindias.

patterns.name: Sikh Gurus in order and their landmarks
patterns.howToSpot: "Which Guru..." with words like Gurmukhi, Amritsar, Adi Granth, Miri-Piri or Khalsa.
steps: Recall the list by number.
Nanak-Talwandi, Angad-Gurmukhi, Ram Das-Amritsar, Arjan-Adi Granth, Hargobind-Miri-Piri.
Tegh Bahadur executed 1675; Gobind Singh Khalsa 1699.
patterns.why: Each Guru has one landmark, and the number in the list gives the order.

example.q: Who compiled the Adi Granth, the original Sikh scripture?
steps: It was compiled in 1604.
The compiler was the fifth Guru, executed in 1606.

patterns.name: After the tenth Guru: Banda Bahadur to Ranjit Singh
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Banda Bahadur, misl, Sukerchakia, Lahore 1799 or five K's.
steps: Banda Bahadur led the Khalsa after 1708. He was executed in 1716.
Misls were Khalsa confederacies.
Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia misl took Lahore in 1799.
patterns.why: The chain Banda, misls, Ranjit Singh follows the tenth Guru in order.

example.q: Maharaja Ranjit Singh belonged to which Sikh misl?
steps: He captured Lahore in 1799.
His misl was the Sukerchakia.

patterns.name: Third Battle of Panipat (1761)
patterns.howToSpot: "Third Panipat", "1761", "Sadashivrao Bhau", "Ahmad Shah Abdali".
steps: Date: 14 January 1761.
Winner: Ahmad Shah Abdali. Loser: the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau.
The Peshwa at that time was Balaji Baji Rao.
patterns.why: A few names and one date solve every question on this battle.

example.q: In the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), the Marathas were defeated by:
steps: Nadir Shah invaded in 1739, so he is wrong.
The winner was Ahmad Shah Abdali.

patterns.name: Revenue terms and posts of the Marathas
patterns.howToSpot: "Chauth", "Sardeshmukhi", "Sumant", "Amatya", "Nyayadhish".
steps: Chauth is 25%. Sardeshmukhi is an extra 10%.
Peshwa: prime minister. Amatya: finance. Sumant: foreign affairs.
Senapati: army. Nyayadhish: justice.
patterns.why: Each term has one number or one portfolio.

example.q: In the Ashtapradhan, which minister looked after foreign affairs?
steps: Peshwa was Prime Minister.
Sumant (Dabir) handled foreign affairs.

revision: Shivaji: Pratapgarh 1659, Purandar 1665, Agra escape 1666, crowned at Raigad 1674.
Ashtapradhan: Peshwa first of eight. Sumant handles foreign affairs.
Peshwas: Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I, Balaji Baji Rao (Panipat 1761). Salbai 1782, Bassein 1802.
Houses: Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Gaekwad (Baroda), Bhonsle (Nagpur).
Gurus: Nanak (Talwandi), Arjan (Adi Granth, executed 1606), Tegh Bahadur (1675), Gobind (Khalsa 1699).
After Gobind: Banda Bahadur (1716), misls, Ranjit Singh (Lahore 1799).

subtopics.title: Bhakti & Sufi Movements
subtopics.concept: The Bhakti and Sufi movements gave the medieval period a religion of love and devotion. Saints sang in the people's own languages and quietly weakened caste barriers. Exams ask which saint belongs to which region, work, language or Sufi order.

example.q: Dvaita philosophy was taught by:
steps: MaD: Madhva gives Dvaita.
Ramanuja is Vishishtadvaita.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Ramcharitmanas a Sanskrit or Braj work.
mistakes.right: It is in **Awadhi**.

mistakes.wrong: Placing Moinuddin Chishti in Delhi.
mistakes.right: Moinuddin Chishti = **Ajmer**. Nizamuddin Auliya = **Delhi**.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Sankardeva is from Bengal.
mistakes.right: **Sankardeva** is from **Assam**. **Chaitanya** is from Bengal.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking all Sufi orders avoided the court.
mistakes.right: The **Suhrawardis** accepted state service. The Chishtis stayed away.

subtopics.notes:
### Two roads to the same God
Bhakti (Hindu devotion) and Sufism (Islamic mysticism) both answered heavy ritual with love and devotion. Both used the people's languages. Both quietly attacked caste.

### Bhakti in the south first
The **Alvars** (devotees of **Vishnu**) and the **Nayanars** (devotees of **Shiva**) sang between the 6th and 9th centuries.

- The **Tevaram** hymns belong to the Nayanars (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar).
- **Andal** is the woman Alvar.

Four schools of philosophy are often asked:

| Teacher | School |
|---|---|
| **Shankaracharya** | **Advaita** (non-dualism) |
| **Ramanuja** | **Vishishtadvaita** (qualified non-dualism) |
| **Madhvacharya** | **Dvaita** (dualism) |
| **Vallabhacharya** | **Shuddhadvaita** |

**Basavanna** (Karnataka, 12th century) began the **Virashaiva / Lingayat** movement and its *vachanas*.

> **Tip:** "RaVi MaD": **Ra**manuja is **Vi**shishtadvaita. **Ma**dhva is **D**vaita.

### North and west India
| Saint | Region | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| **Ramananda** | North India (Varanasi) | Opened bhakti to all castes. Guru of **Kabir** and **Ravidas**. |
| **Kabir** | Varanasi | Weaver. Sayings in the ***Bijak***. Attacked idol worship and ritual on both sides. |
| **Guru Nanak** | Punjab | Founded what became Sikhism. |
| **Chaitanya** | Bengal and Odisha (Puri) | **Gaudiya Vaishnavism**. **Sankirtan**. |
| **Tulsidas** | Uttar Pradesh | ***Ramcharitmanas*** in **Awadhi** |
| **Surdas** | Braj | ***Sursagar*** on Krishna, in **Braj Bhasha** |
| **Mirabai** | Rajasthan (Mewar) | Krishna bhajans |
| **Jnaneshwar** | Maharashtra | ***Jnaneshwari***, a Marathi commentary on the Gita |
| **Namdev, Tukaram** | Maharashtra | **Warkari** tradition. Tukaram's **abhangas**. Worship of **Vithoba at Pandharpur**. |
| **Sankardeva** | Assam | **Ekasarana dharma**. Set up **sattras** and namghars. |

> **Watch:** Ramcharitmanas is in **Awadhi**, not Sanskrit or Braj.

### Sufism: Islamic mysticism
Sufi orders are called **silsilas**, meaning "chains" of teacher to student. The bond is **pir-murid**. Practice includes **zikr** (recitation) and **sama** (musical gatherings). Sama is the root of **qawwali**.

| Order | Key saint | Centre and note |
|---|---|---|
| **Chishti** | **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti** (came c. 1192) | **Ajmer** |
| Chishti | **Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki** | Delhi. The Qutub Minar is named after him. |
| Chishti | **Baba Farid** | Pakpattan. His verses are in the **Adi Granth**. |
| Chishti | **Nizamuddin Auliya** | Delhi. Disciple: **Amir Khusrau**. |
| **Suhrawardi** | **Bahauddin Zakariya** | **Multan**. Accepted state service. |
| **Naqshbandi** | **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi** | Revivalist. Opposed Akbar's liberal policies. |
| **Qadiri** | none to remember | Oldest order. Later linked to Dara Shikoh's leanings. |

The Chishtis stayed away from the court and served all communities. Saints' tombs became **dargahs**, centres of pilgrimage (ziyarat).

**Amir Khusrau** was called *Tuti-i-Hind* ("Parrot of India"). He is credited with shaping qawwali. He wrote in Persian and Hindavi.

### What they changed
- Local languages grew: the Bijak, the Manas, the abhangas.
- Caste lines weakened inside devotional groups.
- Shrines such as Ajmer, Pandharpur and the dargahs of Delhi became shared spaces.

patterns.name: Alvars, Nayanars and the Acharyas
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Alvar, Nayanar, Tevaram, Andal, Advaita, Vishishtadvaita or Dvaita.
steps: Alvars are for Vishnu. Nayanars are for Shiva.
Tevaram belongs to the Nayanars. Andal is the woman Alvar.
Schools: Shankara-Advaita, Ramanuja-Vishishtadvaita, Madhva-Dvaita, Vallabha-Shuddhadvaita.
patterns.why: Two pairs, Alvar-Vishnu and Nayanar-Shiva, plus four schools, cover this whole area.

example.q:
The Alvars of south India were devotees of:
(a) Shiva (b) Vishnu (c) Durga (d) Surya
steps: Nayanars were the Shiva devotees.
Alvars were their Vishnu counterparts.

patterns.name: North Indian saints: sect, language and work
patterns.howToSpot: A saint matched to a language, a book or a place: Tulsidas, Sur, Tukaram, Chaitanya, Kabir.
steps: Language anchors: Tulsidas-Awadhi, Sur-Braj, Tukaram and Namdev-Marathi, Chaitanya-Bengal.
Works: Kabir-Bijak, Tulsidas-Ramcharitmanas, Sur-Sursagar.
Sect: Varkari means Vithoba of Pandharpur.
patterns.why: Every saint carries one work or language, which the options test.

example.q: Tukaram's abhangas are composed in which language?
steps: Tukaram belongs to the Varkari sect of Pandharpur.
Varkari saints sang in Marathi.

patterns.name: Sufi silsilas, founders and saints
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Chishti, Suhrawardi, Naqshbandi, Qadiri, Ajmer, Multan or Nizamuddin Auliya.
steps: Chishti chain: Moinuddin (Ajmer), Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid, Nizamuddin Auliya.
Suhrawardi: Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan). Naqshbandi: Ahmad Sirhindi. Qadiri: oldest.
Terms: silsila = chain, sama = music, dargah = tomb-shrine.
patterns.why: Order, saint and city come together in one line each.

example.q: The Suhrawardi silsila in India is linked with which saint?
steps: Chishti saints avoided state service.
The Suhrawardi saint of Multan was Bahauddin Zakariya.

patterns.name: Shared features of Bhakti and Sufi movements
patterns.howToSpot: "Which is common to both movements?" or a statement question about them.
steps: List the common ground: devotion above ritual, local languages, guru at the centre.
Add: criticism of caste and equality in devotion.
Do not accept extreme claims such as 'both opposed all temples'.
patterns.why: Statement questions test whether you judge each claim, not a slogan.

example.q: Which feature was common to both the Bhakti and Sufi movements?
steps: Both used the people's languages.
Both offered a devotional path open to all castes and communities.
example.answer: Use of local languages and a devotional path open to all

patterns.name: Regional saints: place and work
patterns.howToSpot: "Which saint founded Ekasarana / Lingayat / Gaudiya...?" or a saint-region match.
steps: Sankardeva: Assam, Ekasarana dharma, sattras.
Basavanna: Karnataka, Lingayat, vachanas.
Chaitanya: Bengal-Odisha, Gaudiya Vaishnavism. Jnaneshwar: Maharashtra, Jnaneshwari.
patterns.why: Each saint has a home region, which removes most wrong options.

example.q: Ekasarana dharma, with its sattras and namghars, was spread in Assam by:
steps: Sattras are Vaishnava monastery-centres.
The Assam saint is Sankardeva.

revision: Alvars worship Vishnu. Nayanars worship Shiva. Tevaram is Nayanar hymns. Andal is the woman Alvar.
Advaita: Shankara. Vishishtadvaita: Ramanuja. Dvaita: Madhva.
Kabir: Bijak. Tulsidas: Awadhi. Surdas: Braj. Tukaram: Marathi abhangas (Warkari, Vithoba of Pandharpur).
Chishti: Moinuddin, then Nizamuddin. Suhrawardi: Bahauddin Zakariya. Naqshbandi: Sirhindi. Qadiri.
Sama is music. Pir-murid is teacher and student. A dargah is a tomb-shrine.

subtopics.title: Medieval Books & Foreign Travellers
subtopics.concept: Our knowledge of medieval India comes from court chronicles, memoirs, poems and the reports of foreign travellers. Exams ask which author wrote which book, and which traveller visited which ruler. Learn each book with its author, and each traveller with his country and ruler.

tricks.title: Mughal chroniclers: Abul praises, Badauni bites
tricks.body: **Abul** Fazl wrote the official, praising *Akbarnama* and *Ain*. **Badauni** wrote the **b**itter, critical *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh*.

example.q: Which historian wrote a critical account of Akbar's religious policy?
steps: Critical and bitter points to Badauni.
His book is Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh.

tricks.title: Travellers by century
tricks.body: 11th Al-Biruni, 13th Marco Polo, 14th Ibn Battuta, 15th Conti and Abdur Razzaq, 16th Paes and Nuniz, 17th Hawkins, Roe, Bernier and Tavernier.

mistakes.wrong: Calling Ibn Battuta a Persian traveller.
mistakes.right: He was **Moroccan** and served as qazi of Delhi.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Humayun wrote the Humayun-nama.
mistakes.right: **Gulbadan Begum**, Babur's daughter, wrote it.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the Ain-i-Akbari as a separate book.
mistakes.right: It is the **third volume** of the Akbarnama.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking Al-Biruni came with Muhammad Ghori.
mistakes.right: He came with **Mahmud of Ghazni**.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing Hawkins and Roe.
mistakes.right: **Hawkins** came in 1608. **Roe** came in 1615 as envoy of James I.

subtopics.notes:
### Chronicles of the court
| Book | Author | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind)* | **Al-Biruni** | India under Mahmud of Ghazni |
| *Tabaqat-i-Nasiri* | **Minhaj-us-Siraj** | Dedicated to Nasiruddin Mahmud |
| *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi* | **Ziauddin Barani** | Sultanate history. He also wrote *Fatawa-i-Jahandari*, advice to kings. |
| *Rihla* | **Ibn Battuta** | Travels, including Muhammad bin Tughlaq's India |
| *Padmavat* | **Malik Muhammad Jayasi** | Awadhi epic (1540) |
| *Humayun-nama* | **Gulbadan Begum** | Babur's daughter |
| *Akbarnama* and *Ain-i-Akbari* | **Abul Fazl** | Ain is the third volume of the Akbarnama |
| *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh* | **Abdul Qadir Badauni** | Critical of Akbar |
| *Razmnama* | Translation team under Akbar | Persian Mahabharata |
| *Padshahnama* (*Badshahnama*) | **Abdul Hamid Lahori** | Shah Jahan's reign |
| *Majma-ul-Bahrain*, *Sirr-i-Akbar* | **Dara Shikoh** | Sufism and Vedanta meet; Persian Upanishads |

Other writers: **Amir Khusrau**, the "Parrot of India", wrote in Persian (*Khamsa*, *Tughlaq Nama*). **Isami** wrote *Futuh-us-Salatin*. **Babur** wrote the *Baburnama* in Turkish. **Jahangir** wrote the *Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri*.

> **Tip:** **Abul** Fazl wrote the praising Akbarnama and Ain. **Badauni** wrote the **b**itter, critical *Muntakhab*.

### The travellers' ladder
| Traveller | From | Visited | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Al-Biruni** | Central Asia (Khwarazm) | Mahmud of Ghazni | *Kitab-ul-Hind* |
| **Marco Polo** | Venice | Pandya coast (1290s) | Pearl fishery accounts |
| **Ibn Battuta** | Morocco | Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Delhi | Qazi of Delhi. Book: *Rihla*. |
| **Nicolo Conti** | Venice | Vijayanagara (Deva Raya I) | |
| **Abdur Razzaq** | Persia (Timurid) | Vijayanagara (Deva Raya II) | Hampi's splendour |
| **Athanasius Nikitin** | Russia | Bahmani kingdom | *Voyage to India* |
| **Domingo Paes, Duarte Barbosa** | Portugal | Krishnadevaraya's court | Bazaars of Hampi |
| **Ralph Fitch** | England | Akbar's reign (1583) | First English merchant |
| **Hawkins, Sir Thomas Roe** | England | Jahangir (1608, 1615) | Roe = envoy of James I |
| **Bernier** | France | Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb | |
| **Tavernier** | France | Shah Jahan | Diamond merchant |
| **Manucci** | Italy | Mughal India (17th century) | |

> **Watch:** Ibn Battuta was **Moroccan**, not Persian.

### Vernacular classics
The medieval literary map is many-languaged.

- **Padmavat** by Jayasi: an Awadhi Sufi romance of Alauddin and Padmini.
- **Bijak, Manas, abhangas:** Kabir, Tulsidas (Awadhi), Sur (Braj) and Tukaram (Marathi).
- **Amuktamalyada:** Krishnadevaraya's Telugu classic.

Each book is also a source. The *Padmavat* shows Sufi storytelling. The *Ain* records prices and rules. The *Rihla* shows daily life in Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

### What each source is best for
- **Administration:** the **Ain-i-Akbari** (mansabs, provinces, prices).
- **Daily life and courts:** Ibn Battuta's *Rihla*, Paes on Hampi, Bernier on Delhi.
- **Trade:** Tavernier on diamonds, Marco Polo on pearls, Nikitin on Bahmani markets.
- **Court politics:** Barani on the Tughlaqs. Badauni against Abul Fazl's praise of Akbar.

> **Note:** Court histories praise their patrons. Cross-check them with coins, inscriptions and foreign travellers.

patterns.name: Chronicle and author (Sultanate and Mughal)
patterns.howToSpot: A book title to match with its author, or a match-the-column list.
steps: Sultanate: Barani (Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi), Minhaj (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri).
Mughal: Abul Fazl (Akbarnama), Lahori (Badshahnama), Gulbadan (Humayun-nama).
Match the emperor to the historian before you answer.
patterns.why: Each book has exactly one author, and an emperor's name in the title helps.

example.q: The Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, a history of the Tughlaq age, was written by:
steps: The title names Firoz Shah.
Its author is Ziauddin Barani.

patterns.name: Foreign travellers and the courts they visited
patterns.howToSpot: "Who visited the court of..." or a traveller-country-ruler match.
steps: Use the ladder: Ibn Battuta-Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Razzaq-Deva Raya II, Paes-Krishnadevaraya.
Then: Nikitin-Bahmani, Fitch-Akbar, Roe-Jahangir.
The traveller's country is a strong clue.
patterns.why: Each traveller pairs with one ruler, and the country removes wrong options.

example.q: Who visited the court of Deva Raya II of Vijayanagara as an envoy of Persia?
steps: Persia narrows the list.
The Timurid envoy was Abdur Razzaq.

patterns.name: Regional and vernacular classics
patterns.howToSpot: "Padmavat", "Humayun-nama", "Amuktamalyada" or a language question.
steps: Jayasi: Padmavat, Awadhi.
Gulbadan Begum: Humayun-nama, a woman chronicler.
Krishnadevaraya: Amuktamalyada, Telugu.
patterns.why: Each classic has a language and an author, which the options test.

example.q: The Padmavat, an Awadhi Sufi romance, was written by:
steps: It was written in 1540.
The author is Malik Muhammad Jayasi.

patterns.name: Mughal court literature and memoirs
patterns.howToSpot: Words like Baburnama, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, Ain-i-Akbari, Badshahnama.
steps: Two royal memoirs: Babur (Turkish) and Jahangir (Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri).
Ain-i-Akbari is the third volume of the Akbarnama.
Abdul Hamid Lahori wrote on Shah Jahan.
patterns.why: Emperor, book and volume form a short fixed set.

example.q: The Ain-i-Akbari is which part of Abul Fazl's Akbarnama?
steps: The Akbarnama has three volumes.
The Ain is the third.

patterns.name: Best source for what?
patterns.howToSpot: "Which source tells us about prices / daily life / trade / court politics?"
steps: Administration and prices: Ain-i-Akbari.
Daily life: Rihla, Paes, Bernier. Trade: Tavernier, Marco Polo, Nikitin.
Court politics: Barani (Tughlaqs), Badauni against Abul Fazl.
patterns.why: The question type asks you to match a source to its strength.

example.q: Which source is best for Akbar's mansabs, provinces and prices?
steps: It is an administrative gazetteer.
It forms the third volume of the Akbarnama.

revision: Barani: Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi. Abul Fazl: Akbarnama (Ain is vol. 3). Lahori: Badshahnama. Babur: Turkish memoir.
Travellers: Marco Polo (Pandya), Ibn Battuta (Muhammad bin Tughlaq), Conti and Paes (Vijayanagara), Razzaq (Deva Raya II).
Nikitin: Bahmani. Fitch: Akbar. Roe: Jahangir (1615).
Jayasi: Padmavat (Awadhi). Khusrau wrote chiefly in Persian.
Court histories praise patrons, so exams love the question "who visited whom".

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Which sultan introduced the tanka?" or "who moved the capital to Daulatabad?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Iltutmish = silver tanka and copper jital. Balban = sijda and paibos.
Alauddin = market control. Muhammad bin Tughlaq = Daulatabad and token coins. Firoz Shah = canals.

example.q: Which Delhi Sultan introduced the silver tanka and copper jital?
example.solution:
The tanka was a silver coin
The jital was a copper coin
Both were brought in by Iltutmish of the Slave dynasty
**Iltutmish**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The Battle of X was fought between..." or "who commanded the army at..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Panipat 1526 = Babur vs Lodi. Khanwa 1527 = Babur vs Rana Sanga.
Chausa 1539 = Sher Shah vs Humayun. Second Panipat 1556 = Akbar's side vs Hemu.

example.q: Who commanded the Mughal army at Haldighati (1576)?
example.solution:
Haldighati was fought against Maharana Pratap
Akbar sent an army
It was led by Raja Man Singh of Amber
**Man Singh**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A saint is named, and his book, language or guru is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Kabir = Bijak, Tulsidas = Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi), Tukaram = abhangs (Marathi).
Chishti saints: Moinuddin = Ajmer, Nizamuddin = Delhi.

example.q: Amir Khusrau was a disciple of which Sufi saint?
example.solution:
Amir Khusrau was a poet and musician
His guru lived in Delhi
The guru was Nizamuddin Auliya of the Chishti order
**Nizamuddin Auliya**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Foreign traveller and the ruler he met
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Which traveller came from Morocco?" or "who visited whose court?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Ibn Battuta = Muhammad bin Tughlaq (book: Rihla). Nicolo Conti = Deva Raya I.
Abdur Razzaq = Deva Raya II. Paes = Krishnadevaraya. Roe = Jahangir.

example.q: Ibn Battuta, who came from Morocco, served in whose reign in Delhi?
example.solution:
Ibn Battuta was a traveller from Morocco
He wrote the book Rihla
In Delhi he served the ruler Muhammad bin Tughlaq
**Muhammad bin Tughlaq**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Who compiled the Adi Granth?" or "who founded the Khalsa?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Order: Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan, Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, Gobind Singh.
Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth.

example.q: Who founded the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib in 1699?
example.solution:
The Khalsa began on Baisakhi day in 1699
The place was Anandpur Sahib
It was founded by the tenth Guru
**Guru Gobind Singh**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Which Chola built the Brihadeshwara temple?" or "who sent the navy to Srivijaya?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Vijayalaya founded the Chola rise. Rajaraja I built the Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur.
Rajendra I built Gangaikondacholapuram and sent the navy to Srivijaya.

example.q: Which Chola ruler sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya?
example.solution:
Srivijaya was a sea power in South-East Asia
The Chola who attacked it was the son of Rajaraja I
His name was Rajendra I
**Rajendra I**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The Battle of Talikota was fought in..." or "which sultanate came from the Bahmani?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Vijayanagara was founded by Harihara and Bukka; Krishnadevaraya was from the Tuluva dynasty.
Bahmani broke into five: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Berar, Bidar.

example.q: The Battle of Talikota (1565) was fought between Vijayanagara and whom?
example.solution:
Talikota was fought in 1565
Vijayanagara fought the Deccan sultanates
The sultanates joined together and won
**The Deccan sultanates**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, who handled foreign affairs?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Peshwa = prime minister, Amatya = finance, Senapati = army, Sumant = foreign affairs.
Scindia = Gwalior, Holkar = Indore, Gaekwad = Baroda, Bhonsle = Nagpur.

example.q: In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, which minister handled foreign affairs?
example.solution:
Shivaji had a council of eight ministers
The Peshwa was the prime minister
The foreign affairs minister was the Sumant, also called Dabir
**Sumant**

solvedExamples.q:
Arrange the following battles in chronological order:
1. Battle of Talikota
2. Second Battle of Panipat
3. First Battle of Tarain
4. Battle of Haldighati
solvedExamples.solution: Tarain I = **1191**; Panipat II = **1556**; Talikota = **1565**; Haldighati = **1576**. So the order is 3 → 2 → 1 → 4.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Only 3 can come first (12th century) → options A, B, D remain; 1556 < 1565 puts Panipat II before Talikota → A.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following traveller–ruler pairs is **NOT** correctly matched?
solvedExamples.solution: Abdur Razzaq, the envoy of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh, visited **Deva Raya II** (1440s). The Portuguese **Domingo Paes** is the visitor linked with Krishnadevaraya. The other three pairs are correct.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 15th-century Persian envoy ≠ 16th-century king — the dates alone expose the wrong pair.

solvedExamples.q: The **Mansabdari** system, in which every officer held a rank defined by *zat* and *sawar*, was introduced by —
solvedExamples.solution: **Akbar** introduced the Mansabdari system (1570s). *Zat* fixed the personal rank and salary; *sawar* fixed the number of horsemen to be maintained. Mansabdars were usually paid through **jagirs**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Mansab = rank → Akbar built the Mughal bureaucracy; Babur and Humayun had no time to.

solvedExamples.q: In Shivaji's **Ashtapradhan**, the minister in charge of **foreign affairs** was the —
solvedExamples.solution: The **Sumant (Dabir)** handled foreign affairs and relations with other states. Amatya = finance/accounts; Sachiv = royal correspondence; Panditrao = religious affairs.

practice.q: The **tripartite struggle** among the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas was fought for control over —
practice.solution: From the 8th to the 10th century the three powers fought for **Kannauj**, the symbol of supremacy over north India after Harsha.

practice.q: Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated and the way to Turkish rule in north India was opened at the **Second Battle of Tarain (1192)**. Who won that battle?
practice.solution: **Muhammad Ghori** (Muizzuddin Muhammad bin Sam), beaten in 1191, returned in 1192 and defeated Prithviraj. Mahmud of Ghazni had died in 1030; Aibak was Ghori's general.

practice.q: Which Delhi Sultan introduced the silver **tanka** and the copper **jital**?
practice.solution: **Iltutmish** issued the standard Arabic coins — silver tanka and copper jital — and also organised the **iqta** system and the Group of Forty.

practice.q: The Persian court customs of **sijda** (prostration) and **paibos** (kissing the monarch's feet) were introduced by —
practice.solution: **Balban** raised the prestige of the crown with sijda, paibos and the Nauroz festival, and followed a policy of 'blood and iron'.

practice.q: Price control in the markets of Delhi, supervised by the **Shahna-i-Mandi**, was a reform of —
practice.solution: **Alauddin Khalji** fixed prices of grain, cloth, horses and slaves so that he could pay a large standing army in cash. He also started **dagh** and **chehra**.

practice.q: Which Sultan shifted his capital from Delhi to **Daulatabad (Devagiri)** in 1327?
practice.solution: **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** moved the capital to Daulatabad to control the Deccan, but soon had to return. He also issued the unsuccessful **token currency**.

practice.q: The city of **Agra** was founded in 1504 by —
practice.solution: **Sikandar Lodi** founded Agra and made it his second capital. He also introduced the **Gaz-i-Sikandari**, a standard measuring yard.

practice.q: The Telugu work ***Amuktamalyada*** was written by which Vijayanagara ruler?
practice.solution: **Krishnadevaraya** (Tuluva dynasty) wrote *Amuktamalyada*, about the Alvar saint Andal. His court had the eight poets called **Ashtadiggajas**.

practice.q: The **Battle of Talikota**, after which the city of Vijayanagara was sacked, was fought in —
practice.solution: In **January 1565** the combined forces of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara; Rama Raya was killed. 1526 and 1556 are the first two Panipats; 1576 is Haldighati.

practice.q: The silver coin called **rupiya** was first introduced by —
practice.solution: **Sher Shah Suri** (1540–45) issued the silver rupiya and the copper dam, which the Mughals continued. He also rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road.

practice.q: In the **Battle of Haldighati (1576)**, the Mughal army that fought Maharana Pratap was commanded by —
practice.solution: **Raja Man Singh** of Amber led Akbar's army at Haldighati. Bairam Khan was Akbar's regent at Panipat II; Todar Mal was the revenue expert.
practice.shortcut: Haldighati = Rajput vs Rajput: Pratap vs **Man Singh**.

practice.q: ***Ain-i-Akbari***, the detailed account of Akbar's administration, was written by —
practice.solution: **Abul Fazl** wrote the *Akbarnama*, whose third volume is the *Ain-i-Akbari*. Faizi was his brother (poet); Badauni wrote the critical *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh*.

practice.q: The **Khalsa** was founded at Anandpur Sahib in 1699 by —
practice.solution: **Guru Gobind Singh**, the tenth Guru, founded the Khalsa on Baisakhi 1699 and later declared the Granth Sahib the eternal Guru.
practice.shortcut: The **last** Guru created the **last** big institution — Khalsa.

practice.q: In the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**, the Marathas were defeated by —
practice.solution: **Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani)** of Afghanistan defeated the Maratha army under **Sadashivrao Bhau** on 14 January 1761. Nadir Shah invaded in 1739 and Timur in 1398.

practice.q: The traveller **Ibn Battuta**, who served as qazi of Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, came from —
practice.solution: **Ibn Battuta** was from **Tangier, Morocco**. He reached India in 1333 and described it in his travel book *Rihla*.

practice.q: Tulsidas composed the ***Ramcharitmanas*** in which language?
practice.solution: *Ramcharitmanas* (16th century) is in **Awadhi**. Surdas wrote *Sursagar* in Braj Bhasha; Vidyapati wrote in Maithili.

practice.q: **Amir Khusrau**, the poet called *Tuti-i-Hind*, was a disciple of which Sufi saint?
practice.solution: Amir Khusrau was the devoted disciple of **Nizamuddin Auliya** of the Chishti order in Delhi; both are buried in the Nizamuddin dargah complex. Bahauddin Zakariya was a Suhrawardi saint of Multan; Sirhindi was Naqshbandi.
practice.shortcut: Both are in Delhi's **Nizamuddin** — the disciple rests beside his master.

practice.q: The founder of the **Pala dynasty** of Bengal, said to have been elected by the people, was —
practice.solution: **Gopala** (c. 750) was chosen as king by the people to end anarchy — a rare elected foundation in Indian history.

practice.q: **Nagabhata I**, who repelled Arab invaders, was a ruler of which dynasty?
practice.solution: **Nagabhata I** of the **Gurjara-Pratihara** dynasty (Avanti-Malwa) checked the Arab advance from Sind; the Pratiharas later held Kannauj.

practice.q: The imperial **Chola** dynasty's line at Thanjavur began with —
practice.solution: **Vijayalaya** captured Thanjavur (c. 850) and founded the imperial line; Rajaraja I and Rajendra I carried it to its height.

practice.q: The **Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple** at Thanjavur was built by —
practice.solution: **Rajaraja I** built the Brihadeshwara temple (c. 1010) — a UNESCO-listed masterpiece of Dravida architecture with a 13-storey vimana.

practice.q: Rajendra I took the title **'Gangaikonda'** after —
options: A march to the river Ganga
practice.solution: 'Gangaikonda' = 'bringer of the Ganga' — after his northward march to the Ganga; he then built **Gangaikondacholapuram** as a new capital.

practice.q: The Chola village committees chosen under the **kudavolai** system were called —
practice.solution: The elected committees were called **variyams** (e.g. garden, tank, justice committees). 'Ur', 'sabha' and 'nagaram' are the types of village assemblies.

practice.q: The **Uttaramerur inscriptions**, which detail Chola village elections, belong to the reign of —
practice.solution: The Uttaramerur records of village committee elections date to **Parantaka I**'s reign (10th century) — earlier than the famous imperial pair.

practice.q: In Chola administration, the assembly of a **Brahmadeya** (Brahmana-grant) village was called the —
practice.solution: **Sabha** = assembly of Brahmadeya villages; **ur** = ordinary villages; **nagaram** = market/merchant towns. The sabha's working is the best documented (Uttaramerur).

practice.q: The **Konark Sun Temple** was built by —
practice.solution: **Narasimhadeva I** of the **Eastern Ganga** dynasty built Konark (13th century) — a chariot-shaped Sun temple, a UNESCO site.

practice.q: The **Hoysala** capital **Dorasamudra** is today known as —
practice.solution: Dorasamudra is modern **Halebidu** (Karnataka); the Hoysaleswara temple stands there, and Belur's Chennakeshava temple is nearby.

practice.q: **Prithviraj Chauhan** ruled from Delhi and —
practice.solution: The Chauhan kingdom had two centres — **Delhi and Ajmer**. Jaichand's Gahadavalas held Kannauj.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Cholas traded actively with Song China.
2. Chola bronzes are famous for the Nataraja form.
3. The Chola land survey formed the basis of the revenue assessment.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are standard Chola facts: embassies and trade with Song China, the superb **Nataraja bronzes**, and a careful land survey for revenue.
practice.shortcut: Chola administration + trade + art — all three usually appear together as true statements.

practice.q: Who is regarded as the **real consolidator** of the Delhi Sultanate among the Slave rulers?
practice.solution: **Iltutmish** (1211–1236) saved the infant state from rivals, organised the iqta system, issued tanka-jital and formed the Chahalgani.
practice.shortcut: Aibak founded, Iltutmish consolidated, Balban dignified.

practice.q: The **first and only woman** to rule Delhi was —
practice.solution: **Razia** (1236–1240), daughter of Iltutmish, was the first and only woman sultan of Delhi.

practice.q: Under the **iqta system**, the holder of the iqta was expected mainly to —
options: Stay at court as a hostage
Collect revenue and maintain troops for the Sultan
practice.solution: The **muqti** collected the assigned revenue and kept a fixed body of troops for royal service — revenue assignment for service, not land ownership.

practice.q: Alauddin Khalji identified horses by **branding (daag)** and soldiers by —
practice.solution: **Chehra** (descriptive roll of the soldier) and **daag** (branding of horses) were Alauddin's tools to stop the ghost-soldier fraud in his standing army.

practice.q: Which Sultan shifted his court's perception of royal dignity by enforcing **sijda and paibos**?
practice.solution: **Balban** introduced Persian court customs — **sijda** (prostration) and **paibos** (kissing the feet) — to overawe the nobles with royal majesty.

practice.q: **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** is remembered for all of the following EXCEPT —
practice.solution: The **token currency** was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's failed experiment. Firoz Shah built canals, charity institutions and extended jizya.

practice.q: **Timur's** invasion, which crippled the Delhi Sultanate, took place in —
practice.solution: **Timur** sacked Delhi in **1398**; the Tughlaqs never recovered, and the **Sayyid** dynasty (Khizr Khan) followed.

practice.q: Bakhtiyar Khalji's destruction of the great Buddhist monasteries of **Bihar** happened during —
practice.solution: Ikhtiyaruddin **Bakhtiyar Khalji** swept through Bihar and Bengal in the early 1200s (Aibak's period), destroying Nalanda, Odantapuri and Vikramashila's remnants.

practice.q: **Vijayanagara** was founded in 1336 by —
practice.solution: The Sangama brothers **Harihara and Bukka** founded Vijayanagara at Hampi in **1336**, guided by the guru **Vidyaranya**.

practice.q: Which dynasty did **Krishnadevaraya** belong to?
practice.solution: Krishnadevaraya was the greatest ruler of the **Tuluva** dynasty (1509–1529), the third of Vijayanagara's four houses.

practice.q: Krishnadevaraya wrote the Telugu classic **Amuktamalyada** on —
options: Devotion to God (Andal's story) and governance
practice.solution: *Amuktamalyada* (in Telugu) tells the story of the Vaishnava saint **Andal** and also contains Krishnadevaraya's famous sections on **governance**.
practice.shortcut: His book = Amuktamalyada; his title = Andhra Bhoja.

practice.q: Which Portuguese traveller left a vivid account of **Krishnadevaraya's** Vijayanagara?
practice.solution: **Domingo Paes** (and Duarte Barbosa) visited Vijayanagara in Krishnadevaraya's time and praised its bazaars and grandeur. Nikitin came to the Bahmani kingdom earlier; Ibn Battuta to the Sultanate.

practice.q: The title **'Andhra Bhoja'** was earned by —
practice.solution: **Krishnadevaraya** was called 'Andhra Bhoja' for his patronage of Telugu letters (like the great Bhoja).

practice.q: The **Bahmani kingdom** was founded in 1347 by —
practice.solution: **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)** founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347, with the capital at Gulbarga.

practice.q: The five sultanates born from the Bahmani breakup include **Berar**, ruled by the —
practice.solution: Five heirs: **Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Bidar (Barid Shahi)**.

practice.q: The ruined city of **Hampi**, capital of Vijayanagara, stands on the bank of the —
practice.solution: Hampi sits on the **Tungabhadra** (a Krishna tributary); the site is a UNESCO World Heritage property.

practice.q: The **Raichur doab**, long contested between Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis, lies between the rivers —
